newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs slam Commission delays on fur import ban.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs slam Commission delays on fur import ban.

text.p: Present and former Euro-MPs slammed the European Commission on Wednesday for failing to implement a 1991 EU ban on imports of fur from animals caught in steel-jawed leghold traps.

"This is an act of open defiance by the Commission not only of the views of parliament but of the Council of Environment Ministers," British Baroness Barbara Castle, a former Euro-MP, told a news conference in the European Parliament on Wednesday.
Euro-MP Carlos Pimenta, a leading campaigner against leghold traps, attacked the Commission for stalling over the ban in an attempt to avert trade sanctions by Canada, the U.S. and Russia.

The fur exporters have threatened to challenge through the World Trade Organisation (WTO) the EU's ban on use of the traps, which do not kill animals outright but often break their legs and imprison them until they bleed or starve to death.
Castle said EU trade commissioner Leon Brittan was wrong to insist the free flow of trade was an absolute priority.
WTO rules outlawed disguised restraint on trade, which was not the case here, but allowed exceptions to protect human, animal and plant life, the socialist former minister said.

The Commission, Canada, the U.S. and Russia have been trying for months to agree on "humane" trapping standards which could replace an outright EU fur import ban. The talks have effectively prevented the EU's ban coming into force.

Portuguese Christian Democrat Pimenta echoed EU environment ministers' fears that a draft deal, accepted by the Commission, Canada and Russia but rejected by Washington, "would allow some form of leghold traps to continue to be used".

In a move designed to pre-empt EU foreign ministers' discussions next Monday on the traps, Euro-MPs are due on Friday to adopt a resolution insisting, as environment ministers have done, that a total ban must be in place by March.
The resolution also condemns the Commission for giving "higher priority to trade than to animal welfare".
Another former British Euro-MP, Conservative Madron Seligman, said this was the thin end of the wedge.
"This WTO is the beginning of something terrible if it's going to protect all sorts of malpractices and insist on trade. Is it going to permit trade in drugs, trade in white slavery?" Seligman asked.
